title: Hyperlinks
subtitle: The a element and URL anatomy

whyItExists.short: Links are the defining feature of the web — they connect pages, resources, and people. The anchor element makes any text or image clickable.
whyItExists.problem: Without links, every page is an island. Users cannot navigate between pages, download files, send emails, or jump to sections within a page.
whyItExists.solution: The a (anchor) element with an href attribute creates a hyperlink to any URL — another page, a section on the same page, an email address, or a phone number.
whyItExists.impact: Every navigation menu, call-to-action button, breadcrumb trail, and pagination control is built with anchor elements.

explainModes.beginner: The a tag creates a clickable link. The href attribute tells it where to go. Think of href as the 'destination address' of the link.
explainModes.simple: a href creates hyperlinks. The text between the tags is what the user clicks. href can point to another page, an anchor (#section), an email (mailto:), or a phone (tel:).
explainModes.standard: The anchor element accepts href (destination), rel (relationship), target (browsing context), and download attributes. URLs can be absolute (full address), relative (relative to current page), or fragment (#id).
explainModes.technical: Anchor elements with href have an implicit ARIA role of `link`. Without href they are generic inline containers. Link text is announced by screen readers verbatim — 'click here' is meaningless out of context. rel=noopener prevents the opened page from accessing window.opener.
explainModes.deepDive: The rel attribute controls link semantics: nofollow (SEO signal to not pass PageRank), noopener/noreferrer (security for target=_blank), canonical (preferred URL for SEO). The referrerpolicy attribute controls what Referer header is sent. download triggers a file download instead of navigation; it can suggest a filename. Fragment URLs (#id) scroll to an element matching that id — browsers also update history with pushState.

content.text: The **a** element (anchor) creates a hyperlink. The **href** attribute sets the destination URL.
URLs in href can be **absolute** (full address) or **relative** (relative to the current page):

content.label: Absolute vs relative URLs
content.code: About page About page About page Contact

content.text: Use **fragment links** (starting with #) to jump to a section on the same page by its id:

content.label: Fragment links — in-page navigation
content.code:
Jump to About Jump to Contact

About Us

...

Contact

...

content.label: Email, phone, and download links
content.code: Email us Call us Download Guide

content.title: Opening links in a new tab
content.body: Use target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer" together. noopener prevents the new page from accessing your page via window.opener (a security risk).

content.label: Safe external link
content.code: View on GitHub

content.title: Meaningful link text
content.body: Never write 'click here' or 'read more'. Screen readers list links out of context — write text that makes sense alone, like 'Download the HTML guide'.

content.question: Which attribute should you always add alongside target="_blank" for security?
content.explanation: rel="noopener noreferrer" prevents the newly opened tab from accessing the opener page via window.opener, closing a cross-origin security vulnerability.

content.question: What does href="#contact" do?
options: Links to another page called contact
Jumps to an element with id="contact" on the same page
content.explanation: Fragment URLs (#id) scroll the browser to the element with that id on the current page. They're used for in-page navigation and table-of-contents links.

faq.q: What happens if href is empty or just #?
faq.a: href="" reloads the page. href="#" scrolls to the top. Use href="#" as a placeholder during development, but replace it before shipping.

faq.q: Can links wrap block elements like divs?
faq.a: In HTML5, yes — a is a transparent element and can wrap block-level content. This is commonly used for card components where the entire card is clickable.

faq.q: What is the difference between relative and absolute URLs?
faq.a: Absolute URLs include the full protocol and domain (https://example.com/page). Relative URLs are resolved from the current page location (/page resolves from the root; page.html resolves from the current directory).

examples: Wikipedia uses thousands of internal anchor links per article
GitHub uses fragment links to link directly to specific lines of code
